    Good software engineering practices

    Last updated on 2026-11-11 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 12 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • Why would a newer version of R or a package be faster?
    • Are there any risks to updating R and packages?
    • Are faster implementations already available?

    Objectives

    • Explain why using the latest versions of R and R packages is benefical
    • Search for existing solutions

    Keep R up to date

    It’s good practice to use a recent version of R. As well as new features and bug fixes, several releases have brought significant performance improvements. R 3.4.0 (2017) enabled the just-in-time byte-code compiler by default, so loops and functions are compiled automatically, and R 3.5.0 (2018) introduced ALTREP, which avoids allocating memory for large vectors such as 1:1e9 until it’s needed. Since then, gains have been more incremental and specific to particular functions, rather than across-the-board speedups.

    Similarly, major packages with a performance focus should be kept up to date, as their developers implement speed-ups.

    Keep packages up to date

    The same advice applies to packages as to R itself: newer versions are often faster, sometimes dramatically so, with no change to your code. Package developers regularly rewrite slow functions in C or C++, or switch to better algorithms. Some recent examples from widely used packages:

    • dplyr 1.2.0 (2026): if_else() and case_when() were rewritten in C (via the vctrs package), making them up to 30x faster and using up to 10x less memory. coalesce() was sped up in the same way.
    • dplyr 1.1.0 (2023): arrange() switched to a radix sort algorithm (borrowed from data.table), making sorting character columns up to 100x faster. Note that this release also changed the default sort order for strings to the “C” locale, so uppercase letters now sort before lowercase. Use arrange(.locale = "en") if you need the old behaviour.
    • readr 2.0.0 (2021): read_csv() and friends switched to the vroom engine, which reads files using multiple threads, so reading large files is considerably faster.

    You can check which version of a package you have with packageVersion("dplyr"), and update all your packages with update.packages(). Tidyverse package releases are often described on the tidyverse blog, which is a good place to look for news of performance improvements.

    Before updating, it’s worth checking the release notes: major releases occasionally change behaviour (as with the arrange() sort order above), and that can matter more than the speed-up if you need results to be reproducible.

    Check for existing solutions

    There are over 25000 packages on CRAN, and there may already be existing solutions that address the same performance bottleneck that you are experiencing. CRAN task views are a good place to look for packages related to particular problem domains. The high performance and parallel computing with R task view in particular lists many packages where performance is optimised. Packages that depend on or import Rcpp or cpp11 are also likely to be fast, since they use C++. You can find these packages by looking at the reverse depends and imports listed on their CRAN pages.

    Linear algebra and BLAS

    Many operations in R, such as matrix multiplication (%*%), crossprod(), solve(), chol() and model fitting with lm(), hand the actual number crunching to two standard libraries: BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) and LAPACK. R ships with a reference BLAS, which is reliable and portable but not optimised for modern processors. Optimised implementations such as OpenBLAS, Intel’s MKL, or Apple’s Accelerate framework use multiple cores and processor-specific instructions, and can make matrix-heavy code many times faster without you changing a single line of R.

    You can check which BLAS your R is using with:

    R 

    sessionInfo()            # see the "BLAS:" and "LAPACK:" lines
extSoftVersion()["BLAS"]

    A quick way to see the difference is to time a large matrix multiplication before and after switching:

    R 

    m <- matrix(rnorm(2000 * 2000), 2000)
system.time(m %*% m)

    On a 2025 MacBook Pro with an M5 chip, the above calculation took 1.82 seconds with the default BLAS library, and 0.038 after switching to the Accelerate framework, an almost 50x speed-up.

    How you switch depends on your operating system:

    • macOS: the CRAN installer includes a BLAS based on Apple’s Accelerate (vecLib), but doesn’t use it by default. To switch it on, run in the Terminal:

    BASH 

    cd /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/lib
ln -sf libRblas.vecLib.dylib libRblas.dylib     # use Accelerate
# ln -sf libRblas.0.dylib libRblas.dylib        # switch back to R's reference BLAS
    • Linux (Debian/Ubuntu): R from the distribution uses the system BLAS, so you can install OpenBLAS and switch between implementations without reinstalling R:

    BASH 

    sudo apt install libopenblas0-pthread
sudo update-alternatives --config libblas.so.3-x86_64-linux-gnu

    Restart R and check sessionInfo().

    • Windows: there’s no built-in switch. Advanced users can replace Rblas.dll and Rlapack.dll in R’s bin\x64 folder with an OpenBLAS build. Keep a backup of the originals.

    Some cautions:

    • Results may differ in the last few decimal places between BLAS implementations, because they order floating-point operations differently.
    • Optimised BLAS libraries are usually multi-threaded. If you’re also parallelising in R (e.g. with parallel or future), the two can compete for cores and slow each other down. The RhpcBLASctl package lets you limit BLAS threads, e.g. RhpcBLASctl::blas_set_num_threads(1).
    • A faster BLAS only helps code that spends its time in linear algebra. It won’t speed up loops, data manipulation or string processing.

    For full details, see the BLAS section of the R Installation and Administration manual.

    Key Points
    • Keep your R version and R packages up-to-date
    • Look for existing packages which already implement solutions to the bottlenecks you face
    • Switch your BLAS library if your bottleneck is in linear algebra
